You are transcribing a single early modern English manuscript page. Follow the instructions below EXACTLY. Do not skip steps.

=== TRANSCRIPTION INSTRUCTIONS (follow these exactly) ===
# Manuscript Transcription — Adaptive Method

You are transcribing an early modern English manuscript page written in secretary hand (roughly 1500–1700). This is a research transcription — the results will be evaluated against field-standard CER metrics and reviewed by paleography scholars.

This skill has two paths: **Standard** (for legible manuscripts) and **Scaffolded** (for degraded or difficult manuscripts). You choose which path to follow based on a triage assessment of the page.

## Step 0: Triage
**Before transcribing anything, assess the page.** Scan the whole image and score each factor. Factors marked with **(×2)** are weighted double.

Factors (score each 0=None,1=Minor,2=Moderate,3=Severe):
- Physical damage (water, mold, tears, foxing)
- Scan quality (×2) — resolution, pages per image, lighting
- Hand density (×2) — spacing between words and lines
- Multiple hands — different scribes on the page
- Ink quality — fading, blotting, show-through
- Hand quality — how well-formed the letterforms are

Scoring: Add the scores. For (×2) factors, multiply by 2 before adding. Max possible: 24.
- 0–7 → Standard Path (single pass with alphabet)
- 8+ → Scaffolded Path (three-pass method)

Write down your assessment and total before proceeding. Save it to output/triage.txt.

## Standard Path (Score 0–7)
### Step 1: Build an Alphabet
Scan the whole page. Identify page numbers, headings, recipe boundaries, and the clearest text. Build a hand-specific alphabet from the most legible words. For each letter (a–z), document: how this scribe forms it; 2–4 clear example words; confusion risks; variants (e.g., long-s vs round-s). Note ligatures (th, ff, -es graph, -er graph) and this scribe's specific habits.
Calibrate the alphabet: pick 5 clear words from different parts of the page, transcribe each letter by letter using your alphabet, check each against the vocab reference. If 3+ don't match any attested word, your alphabet has errors — revise before continuing.
Note this scribe's orthographic habits: u or v at word beginnings? doubled final consonants? terminal -e? i or j? Every scribe is different. Do not carry habits from any previous manuscript.
Save as output/alphabet.txt.
### Step 2: Transcribe
Work through the page using your alphabet. For each word: (1) look at the pen strokes; (2) match each stroke to a letterform in your alphabet; (3) assemble letters into a word; (4) if unclear, check against the vocab reference.
Confidence scale: clear/unambiguous → write the word; visible but ambiguous → [word?]; some strokes visible → [b....es]; no traceable strokes → [...].
The vocab list confirms readings — it does not generate them. Read letterforms first, then check.
After completing, verify orthography is consistent with this scribe's habits. → Skip to Output.

## Scaffolded Path (Score 8+)
### Pass 1: Survey and Alphabet
Same as Standard Step 1 — scan, build alphabet, calibrate against vocab, note orthographic habits. Save as output/alphabet.txt.
### Pass 2: Skeleton
Transcribe ONLY what you can read from letterforms. For each word: look at strokes, match to alphabet, assemble. If you can trace every stroke → transcribe. If not → write [...] and move on. DO NOT reason from context in this pass. This produces a gapped skeleton — that is correct.
Confidence scale: clear → the word; ambiguous → [word?]; partial → [b....es]; none → [...]; whole passage illegible → [Passage illegible — ~N lines, reason].
### Pass 3: Fill and Verify
Revisit every [...] gap and [word?] flag: look again for partial strokes; match visible strokes to your alphabet; if you can propose a reading, check against vocab reference (on list → confidence increases; not on list → consider a plausible 1–2 letter alternative that IS on the list and that the strokes support, else keep gap). If still unreadable, leave [...]. The gap is the correct transcription.
The vocab list confirms readings — it does not generate them.
After filling, verify orthography is consistent with this scribe's habits. → Continue to Output.

## Transcription Conventions (Folger semi-diplomatic)
- Preserve original spelling exactly — "physicke" not "physic"
- Preserve original punctuation, capitalization, and line breaks
- Expand abbreviations with supplied letters in *italics*
- Preserve scribal errors — dittography, transpositions, false starts
- Keep the scribe's orthography — u/v, i/j, long-s, doubled consonants, terminal -e
- If the scribe wrote "vpon," transcribe "vpon." The scribe's spelling is the data.

## Output (save these files to the output/ directory)
- output/triage.txt — factor scores, total, path chosen
- output/alphabet.txt — hand-specific alphabet with confusion risks and scribe's orthographic habits
- output/transcription.txt — PLAIN transcription text ONLY. No headers, no metadata, no section markers, no manuscript name. Just the text starting from the first line. (The CER script compares character-by-character — any extra text inflates the error rate.)
- output/notes.txt — flagged readings: line number, your reading, why uncertain, vocab verification

=== PALEOGRAPHY GUIDE (reference) ===
This guide encodes Folger paleography training for semi-diplomatic transcription.

PART 1 — Transcription vs Translation: Transcription = faithful reproduction of what is written, preserving original language, spelling, grammar, structure. Preserve original spelling/punctuation/capitalization/lineation; expand abbreviations with supplied letters in italics; record deletions/insertions/marginalia; reproduce errors as written; flag illegible/uncertain rather than guessing. Preserve scribal errors exactly (dittography "make make" stays; transposed "littly" stays; omitted "presciption" stays; false starts "th the" stay; unusual "Spoondull" stays). Preserve apostrophes (Sheep's, kil'd, approv'd). THE CARDINAL RULE: NEVER FABRICATE TEXT. If you cannot read it, do not write it — mark illegible and move on. A plausible word not on the page is worse than a gap. Never generate from context alone. Never let knowledge of English override reading of letterforms. A transcription full of [...] is more valuable than one full of wrong guesses. If most of a line/passage is illegible, mark the whole passage illegible. [word?] is for words you CAN see but are ambiguous — NOT a license to guess unseen words. Translation (modernizing) is NOT in scope.

PART 2 — Secretary Hand confusing letters: e (reversed loop, confused with o); c (looks like r or t); r (multiple forms, sometimes like v or a 2-shape); s (long-s ſ looks like f without full crossbar; round s at word-end); h (descender loops below line, confused with b); d (looped ascender curving left); f (like long-s but with crossbar); k (elaborate loops); p (special forms = pre-/pro-/par-/per-); th (thorn þ looks like y — "ye"="the"); v/u interchangeable (v at start, u in middle: "vpon"=upon, "haue"=have); i/j interchangeable (j as final in roman numerals "iij"=3); ff at word start = capital F. Reading tips: paleography is not exact; forget modern letterforms and spelling; attention to punctuation; every hand is individual and inconsistent, degrades when hurried; work out pen-stroke direction (thin=upstroke, thick=downstroke); compile your own alphabet; majuscule/minuscule used inconsistently; watch interference from lines above/below; if unsure, write known letters with dots for illegible bits and return later.

PART 3 — Common Abbreviations: A°=Anno; Esq.=Esquire; Imp/inp=Imprimis; Itm/it=Item; lre/lres=lettre(s); Ma^ty=Majesty; M^r=Master/Mister; M^ris=Mistress; o^r=our; p^d=paid; S^r=Sir; w^ch=which; w^th=with; th^m=them; th^t=that; yo'/y^r=your. Word endings: -m^t=-ment; -cõn/-siõn/-tĩon=-cion/-sion/-tion; ~ above m/n/vowel = add m or n (mã=man). Special graphs: -es graph (looped downstroke at word end = -es: poundes); -er graph (hook upstroke = -er/-ar/-or/-re: neuer=never); -ur graph (superscript r); "special" p (pre-/pro-/par-/per-); &c.=etc; xp=Christ; "special" s = ser-/sir. Sometimes something looks like an abbreviation but is not; when in doubt transcribe what you see and flag.

PART 4 — Editorial Conventions (semi-diplomatic): original spelling maintained (incl. u/v, i/j, ff for capital F); original punctuation/capitalization/lineation maintained. Superscript letters silently lowered (w^th→wth). Abbreviations expanded with supplied letters in *italics* (except Mr/Mrs and money l/s/d kept as-is); observe scribe's own orthography when supplying letters. Thorn þ → italic *th*; terminal -es graph → -es. Ampersands preserved. Cancelled words → ~~strikethrough~~; interlineal insertions stay superscript, marked with caret ^ if present. Illegible/obliterated → square brackets with dots for missing letters [b....es]; uncertain reading → best guess [word?]. Accidental obliterations/flourishes/line-fillers not represented. Note changes in hand/ink/script size as textual notes.

PART 5 — Confidence Flagging: key question is always "can I see the letterforms?" If no, it's illegible not uncertain. High confidence: clear, trace every stroke, no flag. Medium: CAN see letterforms but ambiguous (two/three readings) → [word?]; use ONLY when you can point to specific letterforms; contextual guessing is NOT valid. Low/Illegible: CANNOT see enough letterforms → [......] with dots for estimated missing letters; correct for faded ink, water/mold damage, or any reading built from context rather than letterforms. If more than half a passage needs [...], mark the whole passage illegible. Context can raise confidence in an ambiguous reading but cannot substitute for seeing the writing.

PART 6 — Recipe vocabulary: receipt/recipe interchangeable; "Take" opens most recipes; dram/scruple/grain (apothecary weights); pottle/quart/pint/gill (liquid measures); seeth/seethe=boil; decoction; poultice/cataplasm; salve/unguent; cordial; electuary; simples; still/distill; anoint; posset; caudle; pipkin; mortar; bolus; plague water; aqua vitae. Ingredients: Venice turpentine; dragon water (tarragon); rosewater; harts tongue (fern); buglosse; sack (Spanish white wine); claret; suet; mace; grains of paradise; sallet oil; bole armeniac; ceruse/white lead; quicksilver (mercury).

=== YOUR TASK ===
Your manuscript image is at: /tmp/manuscript-runs/run-2-opus-4.8/henslow/agent-3/manuscripts/test-page.jpg
Read it with the Read tool (it supports images). Study it carefully.
Your vocabulary reference (~19,000 attested words) is at: /tmp/manuscript-runs/run-2-opus-4.8/henslow/agent-3/guide/vocab-reference.txt — consult it during the verification step (use grep or Read to look up specific words; do NOT read the whole file up front).
Save your four output files to this directory: /tmp/manuscript-runs/run-2-opus-4.8/henslow/agent-3/output/
Use exactly these filenames: triage.txt, alphabet.txt, transcription.txt, notes.txt

When finished, reply with: (1) your triage total and which path you took; (2) a one-line summary of how legible you found the page; (3) the exact list of file paths you READ during this task (for an access record); (4) confirm your transcription.txt contains only transcription text. Do not include the full transcription in your reply — it is saved in the file.
